entry_points.kicker: 96% Gamay · more reasons to look closely

supporting_claims.statement: Gamay represents 96% of the grape distribution in the official 2024 Beaujolais key figures.

The current specification distinguishes an older northern geological family dominated by Paleozoic granite, schist, metamorphic and volcano-sedimentary formations from younger Triassic and Jurassic sedimentary formations that become important in southern Beaujolais; official terroir research also shows substantial variation within that shorthand.

entry_points.title: How can one grape make the map more important, not less?

entry_points.kicker: 1951 · 1985 · a name larger than its share

supporting_claims.statement: The current Beaujolais specification situates early-release trade before 1951, identifies the 13 November 1951 regulatory turn, records the third-Thursday release rule from 1985, and reports a mid-1980s peak near 500,000 hectolitres while stating that primeur never exceeded half of total Beaujolais production.
Under the current Beaujolais specification, the primeur or nouveau mention is available to red and rosé wines, not white wines.

entry_points.title: How did a wine released within weeks shape the whole region’s recognition?

entry_points.kicker: Whole bunches · CO₂ · three different questions

supporting_claims.statement: Full carbonic maceration begins with intact whole bunches in a closed, oxygen-excluding carbon-dioxide atmosphere, allowing intracellular metabolism in intact berries before pressing and completion of fermentation.

Semi-carbonic maceration is related to but distinct from full carbonic maceration: fermentation of juice released in a whole-bunch vat can generate carbon dioxide around intact berries, so ordinary yeast fermentation and some intracellular metabolism proceed together without requiring a fully established external-CO2 treatment.
Whole-cluster fermentation describes the inclusion of intact bunches and stems; by itself it does not establish whether a ferment is full carbonic, semi-carbonic or neither.

entry_points.title: What does “carbonic” actually tell you about a Beaujolais?

entry_points.kicker: A ducal rule · a modern myth corrected

supporting_claims.statement: A 1395 ordinance issued under Philip the Bold targeted Gamay in ducal Burgundy. CARTA records it as historical wine and economic regulation within its own territorial context, not as a modern Burgundy boundary statement.

entry_points.title: What did the 1395 Gamay ordinance change—and what did it not?

entry_points.kicker: One physical hill · two legal origins

supporting_claims.statement: Mont Brouilly is a physical hill: Côte de Brouilly occupies slopes on the hill, while Brouilly is a separate surrounding cru area. Neither appellation boundary is a vineyard-parcel map, and the hill is not itself an appellation.

entry_points.title: Why does one hill carry two cru names?

entry_points.kicker: Mentorship · employment · a lease · a cellar

supporting_claims.statement: Rosenthal Wine Merchant records that when Robert Michel retired after the 2006 vintage he "leased his prime parcel in the Chaillot vineyard" to Guillaume Gilles and "provided his cave" for Gilles's use. A lease is a tenure arrangement, not a sale: CARTA records farming and use, and asserts no transfer of ownership of either the parcel or the cellar.

Polaner Selections records that Vincent Paris's uncle is Robert Michel, that his first vintage was 1997, that he made his first two wines with his uncle before renting facilities of his own, that he inherited most of his vines from his grandfather, and that he rented and then purchased vines from his uncle including Geynale in the Cornas amphitheatre.

entry_points.title: What actually passed from one Cornas grower to the next?

supporting_claims.statement: The Cornas specification states that "les vins sont issus du cépage syrah N". Cornas is red only and admits no accessory or white variety at all — the single-variety outlier among the eight crus.

Guillaume Gilles Les Peyrouses Rouge is a Syrah wine bottled as Côtes du Rhône, from an old-vines parcel on the flats in the commune of Cornas; Rosenthal describes the site's soils as sand and clay overlain with large galet stones.

entry_points.title: Why isn't a vineyard in the commune of Cornas a Cornas wine?

supporting_claims.statement: The specification records phylloxera devastating the vineyard in 1893, then the First World War and industrial employment draining the labour the terraces needed, until by 1965 only some eight hectares remained. It records the vineyard climbing back past 140 hectares by 2010 after a long replanting and terrace-rebuilding effort.

The Syndicat des Vignerons de l'AOC Condrieu describes Georges Vernay as a man of vision and conviction who "worked hard to rebuild the hillsides and rescue the Viognier grape variety from obscurity", earning the nickname of the Pope of Condrieu. His own estate says he is globally recognised as having saved the abandoned variety and that he replanted his land and revitalised a generation of growers.

entry_points.title: How does an appellation almost disappear — and who brings it back?

entry_points.kicker: Two neighbours · one granite basement · opposite rules

supporting_claims.statement: Saint-Péray is a white-wine appellation covering both "vins blancs tranquilles" and "vins blancs mousseux", the sparkling wines made by a second fermentation in bottle, from Marsanne and Roussanne, over the communes of Saint-Péray and Toulaud in the Ardèche. INAO gives sparkling wine as roughly a tenth of the volume.
The Cornas specification states that "les vins sont issus du cépage syrah N". Cornas is red only and admits no accessory or white variety at all — the single-variety outlier among the eight crus.

entry_points.title: Why is one cru red-only Syrah and the next white and sparkling?
